# Non-simplex fibers preserve the shared-plane stress obstruction

## Result and scope

For every integer D>=4 there is an actual mixed-integer convex body
with three integer coordinates and D continuous coordinates, all
fibers positive-dimensional, with the following properties:

* Every fiber is the same non-simplex polytope.
* Its exact maximum normalized halfspace depth, for all ambient
  halfspaces including oblique ones, is beta=91/320.
* One group of four actual critical caps is a positive continuous-
  normal circuit, covers the entire ambient space, and has a common
  effective-section centroid at a deepest mixed-integer point.
* The normalized cap multipliers satisfy every shared-body-plane
  signed mass and full first-moment equation, and every cap-side
  threshold, integer-normal, and continuous-normal moment equation.
* Nevertheless that one group's multiplier sum is

      320/91 > 3 > 1/Gamma_D,
      Gamma_D=(D/(D+1))^D.

Thus the signed first-moment data in
`candidate d485228e666ca27b` do not bound one group's multiplier
sum by 1/Gamma_D, even with actual non-simplex fibers and genuine
critical caps. The exact obstruction persists under tensoring with
an arbitrary centrally symmetric polytope of positive dimension.
This statement concerns necessary stationarity data, not actual
minimality of the depth among all convex bodies. It is not a
counterexample to OC.

The new ingredient used to certify all oblique halfspaces is the
proved ordinary paired-centroid inequality in dimension three from
`candidate 732b11a769399016` (also proved
with strictness in `candidate d494e7e71949ac0b`).
No mixed-integer lower bound is invoked.

## 1. A precise product rule for moment certificates

Here is the elementary tensor operation underlying the example.
Consider finitely many full-dimensional polytope fibers K_z in R^m,
caps H_j, and nonnegative multipliers lambda_j. Assume there are no
owner ties and no cap coinciding with a body facet. For each shared
body plane, its signed boundary trace measure is

    W_f = boundary trace of the fibers
               -sum_j lambda_j boundary trace inside H_j.

Suppose its total mass and full (z,x) first moment vanish. Also
suppose the signed volume measure

    V = sum_z 1_(K_z)(x) dx at z
             -sum_j lambda_j sum_z 1_(K_z intersect H_j)(x) dx at z

has zero mass and full (z,x) first moment.

Let B be any full-dimensional polytope in an orthogonal space.
Replace every K_z by K_z times B and let every cap ignore the B
coordinate. Every old facet becomes F times B; its signed trace
is exactly W_f times Lebesgue measure on B. Its mass and first
moment vanish by Fubini. Every new facet is K_z times G for a facet
G of B; its signed trace is exactly V times facet measure on G,
so these moments vanish as well. These are all facets of the
Cartesian product. This proves preservation of every required
shared-plane signed boundary moment.

More strongly, for either facet type, multiplying any affine
function of (z,x) by any bounded measurable function of the B
coordinate still gives zero integral against the signed trace.
This follows from the same product factorization. Thus the
construction preserves a conditional family of exact moment
identities, not just finitely many averaged B-coordinate moments.

The volume-moment hypothesis is explicit and cannot in general be
deduced from only the original boundary first moments. It is
verified directly in the construction below.

## 2. The body and its exact integer fibers

In R^3 put

    p_1=(1,0,0),  p_2=(0,1,0),  p_3=(0,0,1),
    p_4=(-1,-1,-1),
    T=conv{p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4},
    P={0,p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4}.

The tetrahedron T has centroid zero and volume A=2/3. Its integer
points are exactly P. One direct proof uses barycentric coordinates
alpha_4=(1-z_1-z_2-z_3)/4 and alpha_i=z_i+alpha_4. For an integer
point in T with all coordinates nonnegative, their sum is at most
one, giving 0 or one of p_1,p_2,p_3. Otherwise write its least
coordinate as -k, k>=1. Nonnegative barycentric coordinates imply
alpha_4>=k, whence sum z_i<=1-4k; on the other hand sum z_i>=-3k.
Thus k<=1, and when k=1 all three coordinates must be -1, giving
p_4. This exhausts all integer points.

Fix k=D-3>=1 and any full-dimensional centrally symmetric polytope
B in R^k, centered at zero. Write V_B=vol_k(B)>0. In coordinates
(z,x,w) in R^3 times R^3 times R^k, define

    C=T times T times B,
    S=C intersect (Z^3 times R^D)=P times T times B.

Every integer fiber is K=T times B. Its volume is A V_B and the
total mixed volume is M=5 A V_B. These are all full-dimensional
continuous fibers, so the measure here is exactly H_D, the finite
sum of D-dimensional fiber volumes.

K is not a simplex. Indeed T times B has at least 4(k+1) vertices,
whereas a D-dimensional simplex has D+1=k+4 vertices, and
4(k+1)>k+4 for k>=1. No assertion about nonpolyhedral boundary
variations is required.

## 3. The ordinary product's centroid cap bound

Let X be uniform on T and W uniform on B, independently. Write
gamma=Gamma_3=27/64. For every linear functional u.x+v.w,

    P(u.X+v.W>=0)>=gamma.                              (1)

If u!=0, condition on W and pair its values W and -W. The average
conditional probability is

    [P(u.X>=s)+P(u.X>=-s)]/2 >= gamma,

where s=-v.W, by the proved paired-centroid theorem for T in
dimension three. Integration gives (1). If u=0 and v!=0, the law
v.W is symmetric and atomless, so the probability is 1/2. If both
are zero the probability is one. Thus (1) includes every ambient
continuous normal, including those coupling x and w.

For every point (x,w) in K, some barycentric coordinate alpha_j(x)
in T is at least 1/4. The halfspace alpha_j(X)>=alpha_j(x), ignoring
w, contains that point and has fraction
(1-alpha_j(x))^3<=27/64. Consequently the exact maximum ordinary
halfspace depth of K is gamma, attained at its centroid (0,0).

## 4. Exact mixed-integer depth, including all oblique halfspaces

The point y=(0,0,0) belongs to S. Consider any closed ambient
halfspace through y. Its contribution from the central fiber is
at least gamma A V_B by (1), or is the entire central fiber in the
purely integer-normal case.

The four outer fibers contribute at least A V_B in total. To see
this without restricting the normal, let R be the affine linear
map cycling the four vertices of T. Since their barycenter is
zero, R is linear, preserves T and its uniform measure, and

    x+Rx+R^2x+R^3x=0   for every x in R^3.

For independent X uniform on T and W uniform on B, couple the
outer-fiber points by

    (p_1,X,W), (p_2,RX,-W),
    (p_3,R^2X,W), (p_4,R^3X,-W).

Each is uniformly distributed on its own outer fiber, and their
ambient vector sum is zero. Therefore at least one member lies
in every closed halfspace through zero. Integrating this indicator
inequality proves the stated total outer-fiber bound. It uses no
independence among the four coupled points and is valid when some
of them lie on the boundary.

Every containing halfspace can first have its boundary moved to y,
only decreasing its mass. Hence the depth of y is at least

    beta=(1+gamma)/5=91/320.                           (2)

Conversely, for any point in the central fiber, choose the
tetrahedral barycentric cap of fraction at most gamma described
in Section 3. Add a sufficiently large integer-coordinate linear
term whose value is positive at one p_i and negative at the other
three p_j. Such a term exists explicitly below. The resulting
closed ambient halfspace includes exactly one whole outer fiber,
excludes the other three, and has the chosen central cap. Its mass
is at most (1+gamma) A V_B.

For a point in an outer fiber p_i, choose the same barycentric
cap through its x-coordinate and add a sufficiently large integer
term exposing p_i strictly among all five indices P. All other
fibers are then excluded. Its mass is at most gamma A V_B, so an
outer fiber has depth at most gamma/5<beta. A large term is finite:
all continuous coordinates range over a compact body and the
strict discrete gaps have positive minimum. This argument needs
no limiting cap or omitted boundary fiber.

Thus beta in (2) is the exact global maximum depth. The central
integer index is the only deepest index, and y is a deterministic
deepest point.

## 5. An actual critical circuit and its effective sections

Put

    u_1=(3,-1,-1), u_2=(-1,3,-1), u_3=(-1,-1,3),
    u_4=(-1,-1,-1).

Then sum_j u_j=0, u_j.p_j=3, and u_j.p_i=-1 for i!=j.
Moreover T={x:u_j.x>=-1 for every j}, so -1<=u_j.x<=3 on T.
Take the four closed caps

    H_j={(z,x,w):10 u_j.z+u_j.x>=0}.                   (3)

H_j contains its own outer fiber entirely, excludes the other
three outer fibers, and cuts the central fiber in the ordinary
tetrahedral centroid cap of fraction gamma. It therefore has
mass beta M exactly. Each boundary passes through y, and the
positive circuit sum of all four margins is zero, so these four
closed caps cover the whole ambient space.

Let c_j=|u_j|. To use unit continuous normals, divide every
coefficient of (3) by c_j, and use

    rho_j=c_j/(sum_l c_l).

These strictly positive weights sum to one and balance the four
unit continuous normals. Their rank is three and the circuit is
minimal. In D>3 the rank is less than D, as is expressly permitted
for a positive circuit of at most D+1 normals. The common integer
projected coefficient A=sum_j rho_j(10u_j/c_j) is zero, so this
one group covers every assigned index.

Only the central fiber contributes a proper section to each cap.
Its section is {x in T:u_j.x=0} times B and has centroid (0,0).
The coarea section mass in the unnormalized u_j coordinate is

    sigma=A V_B gamma,

because the cap volume at threshold s is
A V_B((3-s)/4)^3, whose negative derivative at s=0 is
27 A V_B/64. Thus in unit coordinates its section mass is
S_j=c_j sigma. Its integer and continuous first moments are zero.
All sections are proper, so no coincident-facet allocation or
positive boundary mass is being hidden in these formulas.

## 6. All volume and shared-plane moment equations

Give every cap the multiplier

    lambda=80/91.                                    (4)

Then sum_j lambda=320/91=1/beta. The signed volume measure from
Section 1 has zero total mass, since each cap has mass beta M.
Its integer first moment is zero: the only noncentral mass of
H_j is its full outer fiber p_j, and sum_j p_j=0. Its x first
moment is zero: the j-th central centroid cap has centroid p_j/4,
so their summed first moment is zero. The full fibers have
centroid zero. Every cap and every
fiber also has w first moment zero, because B is centered. These
verify the volume-moment assumptions of the product rule.

For completeness, the boundary equations can also be checked
directly on every actual facet. There are no body-owner ties.

For a tetrahedral facet F_l opposite p_l, only the three caps
j!=l cut a positive-area part of the central F_l. Each such part
is a homothetic copy of F_l with linear scale 3/4, hence area
fraction 9/16. Their aggregate area factor is 27/16=4gamma.
Their aggregate first moment is (27/16) times the full facet
first moment, because permutation of the three facet vertices
preserves the sum and fixes its centroid. The four outer full
traces add a factor 4, with integer moment proportional to
sum_j p_j=0. Thus cap-weighted mass and continuous first moment
on the shared facet F_l times B agree with the objective traces,
since

    lambda*(4+27/16)=(80/91)*(91/16)=5.                 (5)

Integer first moments agree as well, and multiplication by B
preserves every product-coordinate moment required in Section 1.

For a facet G of B, each fiber facet is T times G. The central
cap traces have total tetrahedral volume factor 4gamma=27/16,
and their x first moments sum to zero. The four outer full traces
again contribute factor 4 and zero integer first moment. Identity
(5) therefore matches mass and all x, z, and w first moments on
this shared body plane too. This exhausts the facets of T times B.

Writing the signed trace in the notation of the stress theorem,
omega_f=1 and alpha_jf is simply the cap indicator almost
everywhere. Hence for each shared ambient body plane f,

    integral dW_f=0,
    integral z dW_f=0,
    integral (x,w) dW_f=0.

Section 1 shows in addition that these balances hold after
inserting any bounded measurable multiplier depending on w.

## 7. Cap-side stress and the failed group estimate

Assign the central deepest index to the critical group (3).
Its coverage equality is active and all its cap-section first
moments vanish. Put

    t_group=lambda sigma sum_j c_j>0.

The threshold equation in unit coordinates is then exactly

    lambda S_j = lambda c_j sigma = rho_j t_group.

The integer-normal and continuous-normal equations have zero
on both sides, so one may take the transported deepest point and
the continuous-normal multiplier both equal to zero. Additional
groups isolating each outer fiber have strictly slack budgets
gamma A V_B<beta M and zero multipliers; if an assignment of all
indices is desired, these supply it without changing any equation.

Finally,

    sum_j lambda =320/91 > 3 > e > 1/Gamma_D.           (6)

Here e<3 follows from its positive series, and
(1+1/D)^D<e gives 1/Gamma_D<e. Thus the desired multiplier bound
fails by a fixed exact margin already exceeding 47/91.

The same signed-exponential description available for every
tetrahedral cap, and the stronger symmetric-noise centroid theorem
used in Section 3, are both fully valid on this example. Therefore
using those descriptions cannot turn these satisfied moment
equations alone into the false group estimate. Any successful
extremal proof must use additional information beyond this one
selected critical group's normalized first-order certificate.
